newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour would delay merger of energy regulator.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour would delay merger of energy regulator.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party will not attempt to merge the regulators in the gas and electricity industries until after 1998 if it is returned to power in the upcoming election, Martin O'Neill, Labour MP and chairman of the Trade and Industry Select Committee, said on Wednesday.
And he added that Labour has no plans to change the current natural gas pricing formula, based on an annual discount to the cost of living index, known as RPI - X.
"We have yet to be convinced that there's a better way of doing it than RPI - X," he told a conference.

O'Neill's Select Committee is currently holding an enquiry into the regulatory process, and he said he could not yet comment officially on its recommendations on reform of the regulation of utilities.
But he said any changes would depend on the success of the introduction of full domestic deregulation of the gas industry as well as electricity deregulation during 1998.
"There's better based optimism in the gas industry than in the electricity industry," he said.

He added that as a consequence of the Gas Act of 1995, the secretary of state, the regulator, the industry and British Gas knew exactly what was required of them to be ready for market deregulation during 1998.

"We will have to look closely at the role of the regulator post-1998," he said. "It's likely we will move to a single regulator for energy." But he added that he was not sure yet how this would be done.
He said that Labour party policy is not to take a decision on a single regulator until after 1998.
"There's quite a lot of sympathy for the idea of a single regulator but we won't take a decision until then," he said.
On pricing policy, O'Neill said that imposing price caps can "frighten off much needed investment," and added that RPI-X drives down costs and increases efficiency.

He said it can be an effective way of redistributing profits to consumers if the "X factor" is manipulated appropriately. "I'm not sure if a regulator would be happy to alter the X factor in the middle of a pricing cycle, but he has the power so to do," he added.

On a windfall tax, O'Neill said the size of such a tax would be determined in the event of Labour forming a government, but he added that he thinks "there is little chance of the tax needing to be passed on to the consumer."
Labour will not reverse any of the moves towards liberalisation of the gas market.

"As far as the Labour party is concerned, there is no intention to reverse the process of privatisation or liberalisation. I don't think there will be any changes whatsoever in the basic thrust of the way liberalisation is going," he said, adding that there will just be changes of emphasis.

But he said an incoming Labour government would need to address the consequences of increasing dependency on gas by improving security of supply. This would be done by starting talks with Norway on gas supplies in order to avoid too much dependence on potentially less secure sources such as Algeria and Russia.
